newsitem.title: GERMANY: Waigel says tax reforms to boost growth, jobs.
newsitem.headline: Waigel says tax reforms to boost growth, jobs.

text.p: Finance Minister Theo Waigel said on Thursday that government tax reforms would help Germany meet the challenge of globalisation, accelerate economic growth and boost job creation.
Waigel told the Bundestag lower house of parliament that big tax cuts over the next two years would be balanced out and eventually more than offset by resulting faster growth.
"I am convinced...that such a structural change in the tax system and a cut in tax rates would not lead to a fall in tax revenues, but a stabilisation and a long-term rise," he said.

The Bundestag was holding its second and third readings on government tax reform legislation which would slash income and corporate taxes by 1999 while scrapping a morass of exemptions seen as distorting economic incentives and deterring investors.
In a short speech, Waigel made no reference to Bonn's bid to contain borrowing this year and next to qualify for Europe's single currency, focusing instead on the strategy behind the tax reform.

The huge financial burden arising from German unification is still weighing on the economy and state, he said, meaning that despite expected growth of 2.5 percent this year neither the jobs market nor tax revenues are reacting positively.

"We need to take structural action," Waigel said, adding that tough savings were needed to get state spending as a share of gross domestic product below 50 percent this year, and under 49 percent in 1998.

Waigel's 1998 and 1999 tax bills were expected to pass the Bundestag, but face rejection on July 4 by the Bundesrat upper house of parliament, controlled by opposition Social Democrats (SPD). Parliament's mediation process will then be invoked.
